entry.title: The eight limbs
entry.summary: The phrase that names the sport in English — the art of eight limbs — is a count: fists, elbows, knees and shins, two of each.

entry.title: The elbow
entry.summary: A short bone with no padding on it, swung horizontally, diagonally, upward, downward, off a spin, or in the air.

entry.title: The fist
entry.summary: Punches. Historically the thinnest part of the Thai arsenal, and still the part a stadium judge values least.

entry.title: The knee
entry.summary: The point of the thigh bone driven into ribs, liver, sternum or face, usually with the other man's head pulled down onto it.

entry.title: The shin
entry.summary: The front edge of the lower leg, swung on the end of a turning body. The round kick is the sport's signature, and the shin is the part that lands.

entry.title: The foot strokes the face
entry.summary: The one name in the thirty that says what the movement is.

entry.title: Checking the kick
entry.summary: Lifting the shin to meet an incoming round kick, so that the two bones collide and the thrower takes the worse end.

entry.title: The crocodile lashes its tail
entry.summary: Number nine of the fifteen, and the only one of the thirty whose Thai name is still said out loud in gyms from Sao Paulo to Sheffield.

entry.title: The clinch
entry.summary: Hands locked behind the other man's head, forearms on his collarbones, both men fighting for the inside position — and knees going in the whole time.

entry.title: Breaking Erawan's neck
entry.summary: The last of the fifteen, and the plainest thing in the sport: the clinch knee, named after killing the mount of a god.

entry.title: Hanuman presents the ring
entry.summary: The only technique named by three of the four regional schools as well as by the standard list. If anything in the curriculum is bedrock, it is this one.

entry.title: The fifteen that come after
entry.summary: The second set of fifteen, taught after the first. The Thai encyclopedia's line is that a student works the mae mai before the luk mai will take.

entry.title: The fifteen mother techniques
entry.summary: The first fifteen named techniques, taught as a set. *Mae* is mother, *mai* is a move; the fifteen that come after are called *luk mai*, child moves.

entry.title: The dump
entry.summary: Catching a kick, stepping past a leg, or turning a man out of the clinch so that he lands. Legal here; not legal in most kickboxing rulesets.

entry.title: The round kick
entry.summary: The kick the rest of the world copied. Thrown upward at an angle, cutting under the arm and into the ribs, and named for the triangle it travels.

entry.title: The teep
entry.summary: The straight push with the ball or sole of the foot, into the stomach, hip or chest. The article calls it a foot jab and that is what it does: it manages distance and interrupts.

entry.title: Top maphap
entry.summary: The Lanna display in which a man slaps his own arms, chest and thighs in a driving rhythm. Thai Wikipedia's article on Lanna performing arts names it beside the sabatchai drum as the strong end of the repertoire.

entry.title: The three-pit step
entry.summary: Chaiya's first lesson, and the one thing on its list of seven that is not a strike at all.

entry.title: Muay Chaiya
entry.summary: The southern line, from Chaiya district in what is now Surat Thani. Known for defence: elbows in, shoulders up, and a triangle of footwork underneath.

entry.title: Fon jerng
entry.summary: The Lanna martial dance. *Jerng* means tactics or finesse; *fon* is to dance. It is performed with weapons and with empty hands, and the Thai-language history of muay thai names it as the origin of the craft.

entry.title: The four lines, and the rhyme that ranks them
entry.summary: Four regional schools, each with its own reputation, fixed in a four-part saying that Thai sources still quote first and explain second.

entry.title: Four ways to win a fight
entry.summary: Thai commentary sorts fighters into four kinds, and it is the most useful thing anyone can hand a first-time spectator.

entry.title: Muay Korat
entry.summary: The northeastern line, from Nakhon Ratchasima. The rope was wound to the elbow here, and the punch it is known for travels furthest.

entry.title: Muay Lopburi
entry.summary: The central line, from the old Khmer-Thai city north of Ayutthaya. Its reputation is for angles and feints rather than force.

entry.title: Muay boran
entry.summary: "Ancient boxing": the collective name for what was fought before rounds, gloves and a ring — now performed mostly as demonstration.

entry.title: Muay femur
entry.summary: The all-rounder who fights on timing and distance and is usually ahead on the cards without appearing to try.

entry.title: Muay khao
entry.summary: Built entirely around getting hold of you and kneeing until the round ends.

entry.title: Muay mat
entry.summary: The heavy-handed fighter, looking for the knockout because the points will not come.

entry.title: Muay tae
entry.summary: Built on the round kick, thrown at the arm, the ribs and the thigh until one of them stops working.

entry.title: Muay Thasao
entry.summary: The northern line, from Tha Sao in Uttaradit, tied to Phraya Phichai of the Broken Sword — a general of King Taksin who is said to have been a boxer first.

entry.title: Gao yod, the nine spires
entry.summary: A column of nine spires, placed in the centre of the upper back and running a little onto the neck. At Wat Bang Phra it is the standard first tattoo; other lineages start elsewhere.

entry.title: The rules that come with it
entry.summary: A yant is conditional. The bearer accepts precepts and taboos with it, and the power holds only while those are kept.

entry.title: The mongkhon
entry.summary: The cord headband worn into the ring and removed before the first bell. It belongs to the gym, not the man wearing it.

entry.title: The armbands
entry.summary: Cloth or cord tied round the upper arms, worn through the fight.

entry.title: Sak yant
entry.summary: A tattoo that is a working object: geometry and syllables in an old script, applied by a master, carrying protection, fortune, charisma or fear — and conditional on rules the bearer keeps afterwards.

entry.title: Suea phen, the leaping tiger
entry.summary: A tiger in mid-leap, usually one on each shoulder blade, for strength, command and the turning away of an attack.

entry.title: The dance before the fight
entry.summary: Two halves. *Wai khru* is paying respect to the teacher — kneeling, bowing three times toward the corner. *Ram muay* is the dance that follows, which is the fighter's own and belongs to his gym.

entry.title: The time
entry.summary: A pair of thick bronze cups on a cord, struck together. Closed, they say *ching*; let ring, they say *chap*, and the two syllables are the name and the notation.

entry.title: The drums
entry.summary: Two long double-headed drums played with the hands, one pitched higher than the other. Thai names them *tua phu* and *tua mia* — the male and the female.

entry.title: The victory drum
entry.summary: The Lanna war drum, beaten going out to battle for good fortune and to hold the soldiers' nerve. Three old melodies are named: *Chaiphaeri*, *Chaithiti*, *Chanamarn*.
